attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter, offered as his concession about where LLMs work.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase of the listed real uses and the claim that they are useful. 'Not magical' is rhetorical and correctly left unscored.

contract.note: The plain reading (real, practically helpful uses, not universal or flawless) is ordinary. Using 2024 is a reasonable period for an ongoing observation published in Feb 2025.

evidence.note: A 2024 survey of 9,047 workers reports use for drafting, brainstorming and summarizing, plus reported time savings. It was run by a vendor (UiPath) with Researchscape, so its framing has limits.
HackerRank's 2024 developer survey reports GenAI used for coding, debugging and documentation, with self-reported faster completion. It was run by a company and the gains are self-reported.
Morgan Stanley's 2024 company disclosure says 98% of advisor teams adopted an assistant that searches the firm's internal knowledge. This is acceptable evidence that bounded retrieval use exists.

reviews.rationale: Dated 2024 surveys and a deployment record show real use in every listed category: coding, internal document retrieval, drafting, brainstorming and summarization. They also report practical help. That meets the support condition, which needs only real, useful use. The packet contains no counterevidence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: Keeps 'mostly', 'immediately' and 'intrigued by the idea'. 'Don't want this shit' is hyperbolic, but the abandonment part can be tested.

contract.note: Reading 'mostly bouncing off' as a majority of trial users abandoning soon after first use is the ordinary reading. January 2025 is a reasonable choice of period, and the denominator requirement fits the claim.

evidence.note: A January 2025 survey finds 75% of current US LLM users satisfied. It covers only current users, so it cannot measure abandonment among everyone who tried the tools.
A September 2025 investor analysis of retention curves, mixing consumer and business users. It falls outside the target period and does not measure consumer abandonment after first trial.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures what share of people who tried generative AI abandoned it soon after trying. e1 surveys only current users, and e2 covers a later period and mixed populations. Without cohort data for the target period, the evidence neither confirms nor rules out majority abandonment.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: Adding 'including o1' comes from the very next sentence, which names o1 explicitly. It is acceptable.

contract.note: The speaker gave no measure. Reading 'commoditized' as cheaper substitutes broadly interchangeable across almost all OpenAI models is fair, but whether it means capability, substitutability or pricing power changes the result.

evidence.note: DeepSeek's own preprint claims R1 is comparable to o1 on reasoning tasks. It is the developer's report on its own model, covers only o1, and is not an independent evaluation.
ARC Prize's Jan 2025 test shows R1 far cheaper per task but scoring below o1 at every setting on ARC-AGI-1. That points to a capability gap on one benchmark only.

reviews.rationale: The claim covers nearly all of OpenAI's models. The packet holds a developer self-report and one independent benchmark, both about o1 only. The benchmark shows a price advantage alongside a capability gap. Nothing assesses the rest of OpenAI's lineup, so the evidence cannot settle 'almost entirely commoditized'.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own essay.

semantics.note: The proposition leaves out the universal 'like every generative AI company'. The contract openly excludes that from scoring. 'So commoditized' becoming 'heavily commoditized' is acceptable.

contract.note: Reading 'only ever' as no profitable period, and 'commoditized' as close substitutes with little pricing power, is ordinary and fair.

evidence.note: A May 2025 secondary report on how Perplexity classified its 2024 costs. It concerns gross margin, not the company's net income history.
OpenAI's own disclosure shows a competing AI search product was widely available before the post. That a competitor exists does not show substitution or loss of pricing power.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no verified net-income history showing Perplexity never had a profitable period. It also has no comparison showing close substitution or lost pricing power. The cost-classification report and the rival product launch are only context, so neither part of the claim is settled.
